heading: What kind of change repeats by a fixed fraction?
lead: Exponentials describe proportional rates, while logarithms recover durations and compare multiplicative scales.
outcomes: Verify exponential growth or decay from its rate law.
Distinguish half-life from e-folding time and test a local approximation.

blocks.body:
Two tanks each lose the same fraction of their contents in every equal time interval. The fuller tank loses more material in absolute terms, but neither loses more as a fraction of what it currently holds. This is different from draining both at a fixed number of litres per second. A constant absolute rate suggests a straight line; a constant fractional rate suggests an exponential.

Treat this as a mathematical model: a positive amount N has instantaneous rate dN/dt = kN, with k constant. The sign of k distinguishes growth from decay. We have stated the rate law rather than derived it from a particular mechanism. Radioactive populations, chemical concentrations and temperature differences can sometimes obey such a law, but each needs its own physical justification and range of validity.

An exponential translates equal input increments into equal output ratios. A logarithm reverses that relation, translating multiplication into addition. Together they provide a language for quantities that span many scales and for questions such as how long it takes an amount to halve.

The natural base e is not selected because its decimal expansion is special. It is selected because its exponential has fractional derivative one. This makes the function fit continuous rate laws directly and reveals why logarithms belong beside it.

data.title: Equal intervals, equal ratios
data.caption: The plotted points are N/N₀ = e^(−t/τ) at integer t/τ. Connecting segments aid reading; the exact decay is smooth. Each one-unit horizontal step multiplies the remaining fraction by 1/e.

blocks.title: 1. From repeated factors to a continuous rate
blocks.body:
First divide one unit of dimensionless time into n short steps. If each step increases the current amount by the fraction 1/n, then after all n steps its multiplier is $(1+1/n)^n$. For n equal to one the multiplier is two, while more frequent updates apply later increases to an amount that has already grown. As the steps become indefinitely fine, the multiplier approaches a definite number, denoted $e$, approximately 2.71828.

This construction motivates the natural exponential, written $e^u$ or $\exp(u)$. It is the positive function with value one at zero whose derivative equals itself. Those properties make its instantaneous fractional rate $(d e^u/du)/e^u$ equal to one. The limiting compounding construction and this derivative characterization describe the same function; a full construction is beyond what we need here, but the role of the normalization is essential.

Exponential multiplication follows the addition of input intervals:
$$e^{u+v}=e^u e^v.$$
Zero input gives multiplier one, negative input gives the reciprocal, and adding the same interval v anywhere multiplies the current value by the same factor $e^v$. This is the mathematical meaning of constant fractional behaviour. The absolute increase over that interval still depends on the starting amount.

For a time-dependent quantity, set $N(t)=N_0e^{kt}$. The chain rule gives $N'(t)=kN_0e^{kt}=kN(t)$. Thus this expression satisfies the stated rate law and the initial condition $N(0)=N_0$. The constant k has units inverse time, so kt is dimensionless. The units of N come entirely from N₀. Writing an exponential of a raw dimensional time would leave its value dependent on the chosen clock unit.

If k is negative, the amount decreases but remains positive at every finite time when N₀ is positive. Its rate becomes smaller in magnitude as the amount shrinks. The model approaches zero without reaching it in finite time. Real systems may have detection thresholds or discrete particles; those qualifications concern the model's application, not an algebraic zero of the exponential.

Notice that checking the proposed expression by differentiation is already useful even before we develop general methods for solving differential equations. We can verify a candidate trajectory against a law without claiming that we have solved every possible rate law.

blocks.bridge: Update the amount by a fraction of its current value.
blocks.meaning: Equal time increments give equal ratios, and the constant fractional rate has inverse-time units.
blocks.question: Why does N₀e^(kt) satisfy N′ = kN?
blocks.answer: The exponential differentiates to itself and the chain rule contributes k.

further.question: What is held constant in constant fractional growth?
further.answer: N′/N is constant; the absolute rate N′ generally changes.

further.question: Why must kt be dimensionless?
further.answer: The exponential input represents a numerical scaling parameter independent of the chosen time unit.

further.question: Can positive exponential decay reach zero at a finite time?
further.answer: No. A real exponential remains positive for every finite exponent.

blocks.title: 2. A logarithm recovers the exponent
blocks.body:
Because $e^u$ increases from arbitrarily small positive values to arbitrarily large ones, it has an inverse on positive outputs. Define the natural logarithm by $\ln z=u$ exactly when $e^u=z$. Consequently $\ln1=0$ and $\ln e=1$. The real logarithm requires z to be positive. It cannot recover a real exponent for zero or a negative output because a real exponential never produces those values.

The exponential addition rule becomes a logarithmic product rule:
$$\ln(ab)=\ln a+\ln b$$
for positive a and b. Similarly, $\ln(a/b)=\ln a-\ln b$. A product of successive multipliers is therefore an additive sum on a logarithmic scale. There is no corresponding rule turning $\ln(a+b)$ into $\ln a+\ln b$. Addition of amounts and multiplication of factors are different operations.

Differentiate $e^{\ln z}=z$. The chain rule gives $e^{\ln z}(d\ln z/dz)=1$, so $d\ln z/dz=1/z$ for z positive. The reciprocal slope reflects the fact that a fixed absolute increment is a smaller fractional change when the starting value is large. More generally, for a positive differentiable quantity N(t),
$$\frac{d}{dt}\ln\!\left(\frac{N(t)}{N_*}\right)=\frac{N'(t)}{N(t)},$$
where the fixed reference N* has the same units as N.

The ratio inside the logarithm matters. A measurement of 1000 milligrams and the same measurement of one gram should not represent different physical amounts merely because their numerical logarithms differ. Specifying N/N* makes the comparison independent of unit choice. A different reference shifts the logarithm by a constant; its time derivative is unchanged.

For the exponential model, $\ln(N/N_0)=kt$. Plotting this logarithmic ratio against time gives a straight line with slope k. A straight trend on such a plot suggests an approximately constant fractional rate over the observed interval. It does not alone identify a mechanism, and noise or a changing rate can complicate interpretation.

A logarithm with another positive base b different from one is related by $\log_bz=\ln z/\ln b$. Changing the base rescales the numerical reading. Base ten may be convenient for orders of magnitude, while the natural base makes calculus formulas especially direct.

blocks.bridge: Undo a multiplier by recovering its exponent.
blocks.meaning: Logarithms turn products into sums and their derivative measures fractional change.
blocks.question: Why use ln(N/N*) instead of the logarithm of a dimensional amount?
blocks.answer: The ratio is independent of the chosen unit and has a defined reference scale.

further.question: Is ln(a + b) = ln a + ln b?
further.answer: No. The right side is ln(ab), for positive inputs.

further.question: What is d ln z/dz?
further.answer: It is 1/z for z > 0, obtained by differentiating the inverse relation.

further.question: What does a straight graph of ln(N/N₀) against time suggest?
further.answer: A constant fractional rate over that interval, though it does not prove a specific physical mechanism.

blocks.title: 3. Read time scales and test the model
blocks.body:
For decay write $k=-\lambda$ with $\lambda>0$. The quantity $\tau=1/\lambda$ is a characteristic decay time: after time τ the amount is $N_0/e$, about 36.8 percent of its initial value. It is often called an e-folding time. It is not the half-life, because one half and $1/e$ are different fractions.

To find the half-life H, set $N(H)/N_0=1/2$. Taking logarithms gives $-\lambda H=\ln(1/2)=-\ln2$, and therefore $H=\ln2/\lambda$. The initial amount cancels. This explains why samples governed by the same constant λ have the same half-life even if their starting amounts differ greatly.

More generally, reaching a remaining fraction r with $0<r<1$ takes $t=-\ln r/\lambda$. Reaching one quarter takes two half-lives because a quarter is a product of two halves and logarithms turn that product into an additive duration. The final quarter does not disappear after another equal interval; the model again multiplies whatever remains by the same factor.

Suppose λ is 0.2 per second. Then τ is 5 s and H is about 3.466 s. After 10 s, the fraction remaining is $e^{-2}$, about 0.1353. At that instant the absolute decay rate is $-0.2N(10)$ per second, smaller in magnitude than at the start. The fractional rate remains exactly −0.2 per second throughout.

For a sufficiently short time step h, the derivative gives $N(t+h)\approx N(t)(1+kh)$. This first-order approximation explains the repeated-factor construction. It is useful when |kh| is small, but a coarse decay step with $1+kh<0$ predicts a negative amount and plainly contradicts the positive exponential. The failure is in the step approximation, not the original rate law.

Finally, ask whether the proportional-rate assumption is plausible. A reservoir draining at a fixed pump throughput follows a different law until it empties. Growth limited by scarce resources cannot remain exponential indefinitely. A measured straight logarithmic graph is evidence for a useful model over a specified interval, not a license to extrapolate forever. Mathematics helps us recognize the prediction and the assumptions it depends on.

blocks.answer: Dividing by N₀ leaves an equation only for the fraction, decay constant and time.

blocks.title: The same derivative will govern many kinds of change
blocks.body: Constant fractional growth is not just a special graph. It is the first example of a rate law whose derivative is proportional to the quantity itself, which is why exponentials return in decay, oscillators, Fourier modes and differential equations. The logarithm reverses that representation: it turns multiplication into addition and exposes a fractional rate as a slope. Later, when a physical system is modelled, ask whether the exponential came from an actual rate law or was merely used as a convenient fit.

blocks.heading: Local logarithms for signed functions
blocks.body: For a nonzero differentiable real function f that keeps its sign on an interval, d ln|f|/dt = f′/f. This extends logarithmic differentiation to negative values without claiming that ln f is real there. Zeros still require separate treatment; dividing by f would discard them.

blocks.heading: What survives when the fractional growth rate changes
blocks.body:
A constant fractional rate means that over a short duration $\Delta t$, a quantity is multiplied approximately by $1+k\Delta t$. Repeating the same multiplication leads to an exponential. Now suppose the rate is a function of time. Over successive intervals the multipliers differ:
$$N(t)\approx N(0)\prod_j[1+k(t_j)\Delta t_j].$$
Taking a logarithm turns this product into a sum. When each interval is small, $\ln(1+u)\approx u$, so the sum approaches the accumulated fractional rate. In the integral notation developed shortly,
$$N(t)=N(0)\exp\!\left(\int_0^t k(s)\,ds\right).$$
Every term in the exponent is dimensionless: a rate multiplied by a time.

Consider growth at rate a for a duration T, followed by decay at rate a for the same duration. The exact continuous model multiplies by $e^{aT}$ and then $e^{-aT}$, returning to the original amount. By contrast, a 10% increase followed by a 10% decrease multiplies by $1.1\times0.9=0.99$. Equal signed percentages applied to different starting amounts do not undo each other.

The log of a ratio records the accumulated fractional change and makes such comparisons additive. Later, an exponential solution to an equation will be meaningful because it encodes a rate law. A straight-looking growth curve alone does not establish that the fractional rate is constant.

steps.title: Use the measured ratio
steps.reason: The initial amplitude cancels from the ratio.
steps.trap: Do not take a logarithm of an unreferenced dimensional signal.

steps.title: Recover the exponent
steps.reason: The natural logarithm reverses the exponential.
steps.trap: The logarithm of one quarter is negative, but λ is defined positive.

steps.title: Find the half-life
steps.reason: One quarter represents two successive halvings.
steps.trap: Eight seconds is two half-lives, not one.

steps.title: Predict another time
steps.body: Twelve seconds is three half-lives, so N/N₀ = 1/8.
steps.reason: Equal durations multiply the current amount by the same fraction.
steps.trap: Do not subtract a quarter every eight seconds.

blocks.body: An exponential has a constant fractional rate; logarithms convert its ratios into additive time and scale comparisons.
blocks.nextConnection: Knowing a rate invites the reverse question: how much accumulates over an interval? That leads to integration.

data.coreIdea: Exponential change is the trajectory whose instantaneous rate is proportional to the quantity already present. Logarithms expose that fractional rate by turning multiplication into addition, which is why half-lives, time constants, and slopes on a logarithmic plot are all versions of the same idea.
data.widerConnection: Growth and decay reappear in differential equations, damping, Green functions, probability, and mode evolution. The important transfer is to recognise an exponential as the signature of a local rule that reproduces the current state, not simply as a convenient curve to fit after the fact.
